chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
title: Cliff Jackson's group, harmony study and syncopated tunes
summary: Working with Washingtonian Cliff Jackson, with Hank Larson on drums, Butler studied harmony and learned new syncopated music such as Louisiana Bobo and Archie Bleyer's writing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: No, they were just simple scales. Pass it on the scales. He didn't move no further than that seventh or ninth, then he'd go into the diminish every now and then, but he'd just say right on that, that first -- fourth, fifth, of course, he might make a sixth come down, but you could understand anything he was doing, but he would do so much (unintelligible) and so then now I went -- then I got a job -- I'm a man, I'm getting a mustache and getting side-burns and things, so I got a job working with another man from Washington, D. C. His name is Cliff Jackson, so I'm coming conscious because everybody studying harmony, from a man named Mr. Hall, everybody studying and a boy named Horace Knight was up there. Another man, aged man, his name is Aaron and Cliff is on the piano and a man named Hank Larson on the drum, very beautiful drummer.

So you read and we're getting all these heads and when your music started to change, had a thing called the "Louisiana Bobo," it had syncopation and Archie Bleyer was writing a lot of things that had syncopation, lot of syncopation and that's the first time we seen -- and it was a school for me.
Do you remember the way any of those pieces went?

Like (humming) that was the Louisiana Bleyer Bobo. And Archie had a thing called Saturday Night something, but it was all (humming) crazy rhythm and some other stuff, but at that time rhythm was going on, see (humming) 'Putting on the Ritz,' all this is going in these shows. This is when Gershwin was writing all this beautiful music.
